title: The event loop: why setTimeout(fn, 0) runs last
objectives: Predict the order of synchronous code, promise callbacks and timers
Explain the call stack, task queue and microtask queue

blocks.markdown:
A timer of **0 milliseconds** sounds like it should fire immediately. Yet in JavaScript it often fires after code written below it.

Here is why: JavaScript executes all synchronous code first on its single call stack. When synchronous code finishes, it drains high-priority **microtasks** (like `Promise.then` callbacks). Only after microtasks are completely empty does it pull from the macrotask queue (like `setTimeout` timer callbacks).

Keep that execution order in mind as you predict the output below.

blocks.explanation:
1. Synchronous 'A' and 'D' run immediately on the call stack.
2. When the stack clears, microtask 'C' (Promise.then callback) runs before any macrotasks.
3. Finally, macrotask 'B' (setTimeout callback) runs from the task queue.
Final output: A, D, C, B.

blocks.title: Four lines, three destinations

steps.title: Runs now
steps.narration: console.log('A') is ordinary synchronous code: it runs immediately.

steps.title: Handed to the browser
steps.narration: setTimeout gives the callback to the browser's timer. When the timer expires, the callback joins the task queue.

steps.title: A microtask
steps.narration: The promise is already resolved, so .then queues its callback in the microtask queue.

steps.title: Runs now
steps.narration: console.log('D') is synchronous too, so it prints before either queue gets a turn.

blocks.title: The loop at work

steps.title: The script starts
steps.narration: The whole script runs as the first task, on the call stack.

steps.title: Log A
steps.narration: console.log('A') runs and returns at once.

steps.title: Start the timer
steps.narration: setTimeout hands the callback to the browser and returns immediately; the script doesn't wait.

steps.title: The timer expires
steps.narration: The timer expires straight away, so the browser puts its callback in the task queue, where it waits its turn.

steps.title: Queue the promise callback
steps.narration: The promise is already resolved, so its callback goes straight to the microtask queue.

steps.title: Log D
steps.narration: console.log('D') runs. Both callbacks are still waiting.

steps.title: The stack empties
steps.narration: The script finishes and the call stack is empty. Now the loop drains every microtask before taking the next task.

steps.title: Microtasks first
steps.narration: The promise callback runs and logs C.

steps.title: Then the next task
steps.narration: With the microtask queue empty, the loop takes the oldest task: the timer callback logs B.

steps.title: Resolved
steps.narration: resolve(value) moves the promise from pending to fulfilled, and queues its .then callbacks as microtasks.

steps.title: Too late to reject
steps.narration: A settled promise never changes again: calling reject now does nothing.

blocks.text: Promise callbacks wait in the {{q1}} queue, which is emptied {{q2}} the next task runs. setTimeout callbacks wait in the {{q3}} queue.
blocks.explanation: After every task the loop runs all microtasks, then takes one task. That is why promise callbacks beat timers.

blocks.title: The rule
blocks.text: Run the current task to the end, then every microtask, then the next task. Rendering happens between tasks, so long tasks freeze the page.

blocks.question: What logs first?
blocks.explanation: queueMicrotask adds a microtask, and microtasks run before the next task, even one queued earlier.

cards.front: In which order does the event loop run tasks and microtasks?
cards.back: It finishes the current task, runs every queued microtask, then takes the next task.

cards.front: Which queue do promise callbacks (.then, await continuations) go to?

cards.back: Only that fn runs in a later task, after the current code and its microtasks; never immediately.

cards.front: Can a fulfilled promise become rejected?
cards.back: No. Once settled, a promise never changes state.
